title: The box office movie industry is dying. Number of tickets sold in 2023 are almost at half of their peak in 2001.

commenti.body: Why do movies need to be at a theater to be talked about? I enjoy going to the theater for sure but it’s not like there’s any real difference between gathering around the water cooler and talking about a movie seen on streaming vs one on the big screen? Like the shared cultural context isn’t going to be lost if people don’t go to movie theaters.

I used to go the theater once, twice a week a few years ago.   
I can't afford to live in the metro hub of my city and have to live on the edges, where the nearest movie theater is miles away. The city ones, that play the independent films, are hard to get to.   
The multiplexes are in malls, and public transport drops me off nowhere near the theater. I have to walk up a busy highways, clinging to the side of the rail, to watch these films.   


In addition to the lack of decorum and management of the theaters. Went to see Barbie in a packed theater. A dad in the front row was on his Ipad the whole god damn time. Hundreds of us were distracted by his bright dumb light because 0 people told him to turn of the god damn device. And he had the nerve to ask his family 'if they enjoyed the movie.' Drop your wife and daughter off and go get drunk at Chili's.  
Only go to the theater when you want to watch a movie. I thought that was easy but I guess it's near impossible for people.   


Things need to seriously change if theaters want to continue to exist. Theaters will always exist, but we're going to continue to see a drop in interest if there's not a sea change in attitude.   
Alamo Drafthouse style (sans the personal food service, not every movie should be accompanied by a bourbon burger).   


Also assigned seats sort of suck and can take the enjoyment out of the experience. Because it's still first come first serve, but if you did it on your phone, your prioritized, even in front the people who physically showed up early.   


Film is an active participatory medium. You are meant to think and be challenged. Even blockbusters. The lean back seats add to the jangling keys feel of modern blockbuster film making.

Lot of factors, but I recently made the decision to avoid cinemas for the most part for these two reasons:

1. People forgot how to behave. Not that ling ago, it was a rarity that someone would talk loudly or use their phone in a dark theater. Now, it seems common and almost accepted. Tickets are too expensive for that nonsense.
2. Theater chains don't seem to care. Customer care/service is low pretty much everywhere now, but the chain theaters are commonly dirty, meaning the floor and the screen itself. Weird smells, dirty screens, apathetic people, and outrageous prices.

Meh. My TV and soundbar are quality enough to not put up with the cinema.

When I was a kid watching movies on VHS on a tiny 4:3 cathode ray stereo TV, they were a pale imitation of the real thing on the big screen. You had to go to the movies to get the proper experience.

Now that people have huge widescreen surround-sound home theatre set-ups (maybe even in 4K) there's not such a difference to the cinema experience. There's not such a pressing need to head to the cinema.
I agree with you and prefer my 65 inch in the comfort of my living room.  This post isn’t so much a defense of box office as it is a cultural observation about the industry and its effects.

I think this is a big reason. And it doesn’t help that we have soaked so much money into these systems and the ongoing monthly content streaming. Going to a theater is a pretty big expense to swallow on top of this.

Back in the 90s large swaths of the population would watch a blockbuster on opening weekend, or the week after.  That meant there was a relevant, recent topic of conversation.  Today, with on-demand it's harder to have these common cultural touchpoints.  The movie might be in my Netflix queue but I might not get to it for another few months.

To be clear, as a consumer, I love on-demand.  But it's shifting the culture.

I want to support films and I buy tickets to see the movies I'm interested in, but I'm just not as interested in most modern movies. 

Its a shame because I really love going to see movies in theatres. Poor Things was fantastic and honestly such a treat to see, it bummed me out how few movies have really got me excited lately.

When the majority of box office revenue hinges on whether a marvel movie succeeds or not, I'm not surprised noones going to the theaters anymore.

The average person does not have that or even care to. The average person watches movies on streaming services where the “4K” isn’t 4K and the “HD” isn’t even HD, where the audio is compressed to all hell, often viewed on a small cell phone screen as just one in a million throwaway movies in the heap of ever growing “content”. They’re often watched while doing other things like scrolling social media and playing games. 

Going to the theater gives even the bad films more importance, even renting a movie gives it more significance than tapping on one out of a million movies existing in the ether. 

As far as having a theater-like (or better?) experience at home, the ceiling has never been this high (as well as never been as accessible), but the floor has also never been this low.

I worked at a movie theater for 25 years. Met my wife there, lifelong friends. I'm a lifelong movie fanatic. I've seen one movie in theaters in the past six months and I don't miss it at all. Your points are perfectly stated and I couldn't agree more. Prices, rude people, commercials and trailers for 25 minutes? I used to go every week at least once but now my basement, 75" and 4K are all I need. I know I'm not alone.

I love the big screen so much. Watching *Godzilla: Minus One* in theaters was so awesome—hearing how big Godzilla was. But, I cannot enjoy myself for some reason. The workers don’t care—they rush me through concessions. Everything is so overpriced. Damn near $20 for a ticket? I’ll just buy the film when it comes on Blu-ray. Popcorn is way too expensive, you have to buy the seasoning for it if you want some, and even drinks are expensive. I feel buyers remorse by the time I’m watching the previews.

It definitely feels like a regional thing. My local cinemas are in small towns, nothing major population-wise, and 95% of screenings have no issue with people. The odd asshole usually shuts up quickly when asked once to be quiet. 

They're small, regional chains and the staff genuinely do care. Screens are always clean, can get cheap tickets, and while the snacks can be pricey they don't really care if you bring your own in.

I've seen 12 films at the cinema so far this year already, and even though some of those have been bad films, I've never had a bad time. I'm aware my situation may be fortunate compared to many, but I'll go and support those theatres as much as I can. There's really nothing like a film on the big screen for me.

I agree with you on several points.

We have a smaller theater near us that we go to sometimes. Prices are the only major factor with them; not unreasonable at all, but still more than I really want to spend nowadays. The place is clean, the people are nicer, and the chairs are so much comfier and well-maintained as compared to the large chains.

As for the big screen, that's what I love about going to the movies. Some movies, IMO are an absolute must. But if doing so means putting up with the dregs of society, I'll pass.

Another major factor is that there are fewer quality films to draw people to a theater. The last movie I saw in a theater was Oppenheimer, and before that, The Batman. I can't think of anything else over the last few years that would have been worth going out of my way to see in that format. 

Most of the 'big' movies as of late are CGI schlock. Marvel crap and Avatar sequels are not enough to draw my interest. Perhaps others feel the same. I look forward to Dune 2, but that may be the only time I step foot in a theater this year.

I hear you, and I agree. Recently, I went and saw Godzilla Minus-1 and it brought back what a true theatre experience was, you simply can't beat the large screen. That being said I'm also very aware of the downsides, rude loud people, watching their phones as the movie plays ( man, that always floors me ), and the big one ( which you commented ) - the movies themselves. Give us good movies and we will go and see them, and don't get me started on the movie trailers...Lol.
